p: Dr Johnson, who said a great many things worth repeating and some worth forgetting, remarked that there are few ways in which a man can be more innocently employed than in getting money. He was speaking of trade as against war, and he had a point. But money itself is a stranger thing than most of those who employ themselves in getting it suppose. A sovereign of gold, such as I have in my waistcoat pocket, is worth a pound because everyone agrees that it is; a note of the Bank of England, which is mere paper, is worth a pound because everyone trusts that the Bank will honour it. Money is a promise that society makes to itself, and it works only so long as the promise is believed.

The economists of my century, following Adam Smith, the Scottish author of the Wealth of Nations, have generally supposed that before money there was barter: that the primitive man who had a surplus of fish and wanted a pair of shoes went in search of a shoemaker who wanted fish, and, finding this inconvenient, invented money to save himself the trouble. It is a pleasing story and it has the merit of being simple. The Encyclopaedia informs me that the anthropologists of the twentieth century looked for a society that lived by barter in this way, and could not find one. Within small communities, people do not trade fish for shoes on the spot; they give, and remember, and expect a return later. Credit, in other words, and debts recorded in memory or on tally sticks, seem to have come long before coins. Barter appears chiefly between strangers, or among people who are accustomed to money and have temporarily run out of it, as in a prison.

In the temples and palaces of Mesopotamia, five thousand years ago, accounts were kept in measures of barley and weights of silver. A shekel was at first a weight, not a coin. Debts were recorded on clay tablets, with interest, and the kings of Babylon from time to time proclaimed a general cancellation of debts, to prevent the poor from sinking into slavery. The Hebrew scriptures preserve a similar custom in the law of the jubilee year, when debts were to be forgiven and land returned. Money and debt, it seems, are twins, and the problem of debt is older than the coin.

Many peoples have used things other than metal as money: cattle, which is why the Latin word for money, pecunia, comes from pecus, meaning a flock; salt, from which we may have our word salary; and especially the shells of a small sea snail called the cowrie, gathered in the Maldive Islands and used as money across much of Africa and Asia for thousands of years. In China the earliest bronze coins were cast in the shape of cowries, and in the shapes of spades and knives, the older objects of exchange.

The coin as we know it, a piece of metal of standard weight stamped with a mark of authority, was invented in the kingdom of Lydia, in the west of what is now Turkey, about two thousand six hundred years ago. The first Lydian coins were made of electrum, a natural mixture of gold and silver found in the rivers of that country, and were stamped with the head of a lion. Their great advantage was that one need not weigh them or test their purity at every exchange; the stamp of the king vouched for both. The last king of Lydia, Croesus, became a proverb for wealth, and is said to have been the first to strike separate coins of pure gold and pure silver. As rich as Croesus is still said in English, though few who say it could tell you who he was.

The Greek cities adopted coinage with enthusiasm, and every city struck its own, with its own emblem: the owl of Athens, the tortoise of Aegina, the winged horse of Corinth. Coins made possible the market, where any free man might buy and sell small quantities of goods, and some historians believe that coinage helped to make possible the Greek city itself, with its paid soldiers and paid jurors and its sense that every citizen was an equal participant in a common life. The Romans spread coinage across their whole empire, and their emperors used it to advertise their faces, titles and victories to every subject. It was the newspaper of the ancient world.

Paper money was invented in China. Merchants under the Tang dynasty, wishing to avoid the weight of strings of bronze coins, deposited them with trusted houses and took paper receipts instead, which passed from hand to hand. Under the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago, the government took over the issue of paper notes. Marco Polo, the Venetian traveller, described with amazement how the Great Khan of the Mongols made money out of the bark of mulberry trees, and how everyone accepted it on pain of death. The Chinese also discovered, before anyone else, the chief danger of paper money: that a government in need can print too much of it, until it is worthless. The Mongol and Ming paper notes both ended in ruin.

In Europe, banking was developed by the merchants of Italy in the later Middle Ages, and our very word bank comes from the Italian banco, meaning a bench, on which the money-changers did their business. The Bank of England was founded in sixteen ninety-four to lend money to King William the Third for his wars against France. And it is the Bank of England whose notes, today, form the money of the most commercial nation on earth, backed, since the Bank Charter Act of eighteen forty-four, by its reserve of gold.

The pages from the future inform me that this golden backing will not last. In the great wars of the twentieth century and the troubles between them, the gold standard was abandoned, and by nineteen seventy-one, when the United States of America ceased to exchange its dollars for gold, the money of the whole world rested on nothing but the credit of governments. Most money in the future, I am told, will not be paper either, but numbers in the memory of calculating machines, moved from one account to another by a touch upon a little glass tablet which every person carries. Some of the men of the future have even invented private moneys of their own, kept by a kind of universal public ledger of machines, which they call by the name of crypto-currency, from a Greek word meaning hidden. I do not pretend to understand it. But I observe that it, too, is worth only what people believe it is worth. In that respect nothing has changed since the cowrie shell.
